The quiet harbour town kept its old rhythms through every season. In the morning the fishermen
pushed their boats into the grey water and the gulls followed them out past the breakwater. By
noon the market along the front was crowded with carts of silver fish, baskets of bread, and
crates of early fruit carried down from the hills. Children ran between the stalls while their
mothers argued prices with the sellers and the smell of salt and tar hung over everything. Later,
when the light began to soften, the boats returned heavy with the day's catch and the whole shore
turned out to meet them. Nets were hauled and mended, the fish were weighed and sold, and the men
sat together on the stone wall to count what the sea had given them. It was never a great fortune,
but it was steady, and the town had learned long ago that steadiness was its own kind of wealth.
On the clear evenings the older people walked out to the point and watched the sun fall behind the
far islands, and they spoke of the years when the fishing had been richer, and of the storms that
had taken good boats and good men, and of the children who had grown and gone to the cities and
rarely wrote. The young ones listened without quite believing, certain that their own lives would
be larger. Yet most of them stayed, married, and took up the same nets, and in time stood on the
same wall counting the same modest catch, and found, to their surprise, that it was enough.
